modules.title: Reading Closely and Writing to Learn: How Do Complex Characters Develop Through Their Interactions?
modules.description: Students engage with poetry, fiction, and literary nonfiction to explore how complex characters develop through their interactions, and how these interactions develop central ideas such as identity, honor, and societal expectations. Beginning with a pastoral dialogue across three centuries (Marlowe, Raleigh, Williams), students transition to Ethan Canin's 'The Palace Thief' exploring moral compromise and classical virtue, and conclude with H.G. Bissinger's 'Friday Night Lights' examining community identity and the pressure of expectation.

modules.title: The Power of Persuasion: Rhetoric, Claims, and Human Rights
modules.description: Students read, discuss, and analyze foundational informational texts and speeches focusing on how authors use rhetoric and word choice to develop claims about justice and human rights. Students examine Martin Luther King, Jr.'s 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' to analyze argument structure and rhetorical appeals, Julia Alvarez's 'A Genetics of Justice' to explore the personal impact of totalitarianism and memory, and seminal human rights documents including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Eleanor Roosevelt's historic address.

modules.description: Students engage in an iterative, inquiry-based research process exploring complex ethical questions that have multiple positions and perspectives. Anchored in Rebecca Skloot's 'The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks', students investigate informed consent, tissue ownership, racial disparities in medical research, and scientific ethics, formulating inquiry questions, gathering and vetting academic sources, and drafting a comprehensive research-based argument essay.

White's personal narrative essay 'Death of a Pig' as a study in tragic structure and tone, immerse themselves in William Shakespeare's masterpiece 'The Tragedy of Macbeth', and conclude with excerpts from Niccolò Machiavelli's 'The Prince' analyzing political leadership and ruthless pragmatism.

11th Grade.overview: Grade 11 ELA focuses on complex interactions of plot and character in dramatic tragedy (Shakespeare's Hamlet), seminal American rhetoric on emancipation and civil rights (Du Bois, Washington, Jefferson), women's suffrage and maternal heritage (Stanton, Lorde), rigorous inquiry-based research, and psychological realism in modern narrative craft (O'Brien, Erdrich, Chopin).

modules.title: Interactions of Elements, Tragic Flaw, and Gender Autonomy
modules.description: Students read, discuss, and analyze literary and nonfiction texts focusing on how authors relate textual elements such as plot, character, and central ideas within a text. Beginning with Robert Browning's dramatic monologue 'My Last Duchess', students examine jealousy, aesthetic control, and power. Students then transition to William Shakespeare's masterwork 'The Tragedy of Hamlet', analyzing dramatic tragedy, soliloquies, feigned madness, and moral corruption. The module concludes with Virginia Woolf's seminal feminist essay 'A Room of One's Own' investigating social conditions, material independence, and the tragic fate of Shakespeare's hypothetical sister.

modules.title: Rhetoric, Identity, and Agency in American Democracy
modules.description: Students read, discuss, and analyze seminal historical and literary texts, focusing on how authors use word choice, rhetorical devices, and structural design to develop ideas and advance their points of view. Students begin with W.E.B. Du Bois's 'The Souls of Black Folk' and Booker T. Washington's 'Atlanta Compromise Speech', exploring contrasting visions for African American emancipation and civil advancement in post-Reconstruction America, alongside Thomas Jefferson's foundational 'Declaration of Independence'. The module concludes with Elizabeth Cady Stanton's historic Seneca Falls Address and Audre Lorde's 'From the House of Yemanjá', examining female agency, suffrage, and maternal heritage.

modules.title: Narrative Technique, Selfhood, and Social Awakening
modules.description: Students read, discuss, and analyze modern American fiction, exploring narrative craft, point of view, psychological realism, and personal awakening against societal expectations. Students begin with two masterful short stories exploring war trauma, guilt, and brotherhood: Tim O'Brien's 'On the Rainy River' (The Things They Carried) and Louise Erdrich's 'The Red Convertible'. The module culminates in Kate Chopin's groundbreaking novel 'The Awakening', examining Edna Pontellier's quest for individual autonomy, emotional liberation, and the seductive, untamed voice of the sea.

12th Grade.overview: Grade 12 ELA focuses on personal narrative self-transformation and college essay writing (The Autobiography of Malcolm X, Leslie Marmon Silko), civic resistance and Roman tragedy (Thoreau's Civil Disobedience, Shakespeare's Julius Caesar), global anthropological inquiry (Jared Diamond's Guns, Germs, and Steel), and the conflict between illusion, desire, and cross-cultural identity (Tennessee Williams's A Streetcar Named Desire, Nikolai Gogol's The Overcoat, Jhumpa Lahiri's The Namesake).

modules.title: Personal Narrative, Cultural Heritage, and Self-Definition
modules.description: Students read, discuss, and analyze nonfiction personal narratives, focusing on how authors use structure, style, and content to craft narratives that develop complex experiences, ideas, and descriptions of individuals. Students begin with The Autobiography of Malcolm X (as told to Alex Haley), analyzing racial inequality, self-transformation, and ideological evolution. Students then examine Leslie Marmon Silko's 'Yellow Woman and a Beauty of the Spirit', investigating Pueblo heritage and spiritual aesthetics, culminating in a dedicated college application personal essay writing workshop.

modules.title: Civil Resistance, Power, and Roman Tragedy
modules.description: Students read and analyze literary nonfiction and classical drama, examining how texts treat similar central ideas of authority, civic obligation, and political power. Students begin by reading Benazir Bhutto's 2007 speech 'Ideas Live On' alongside Henry David Thoreau's seminal essay 'Civil Disobedience', analyzing rhetorical appeals and the duty of individuals in the face of state injustice. Students then immerse themselves in William Shakespeare's 'The Tragedy of Julius Caesar', examining the psychological motivations of conspirators, persuasive rhetoric (Antony's forum speech), and the collapse of the Roman Republic.

modules.title: Anthropological Inquiry and Global Argumentation
modules.description: Students engage in an iterative, inquiry-based research process that serves as the basis of a culminating research-based argument paper. Anchored in Jared Diamond's Pulitzer Prize-winning 'Guns, Germs, and Steel', students explore environmental determinants of human history, continental axes, food production, and technology. Students formulate complex inquiry questions, gather and vet academic sources, track counterclaims, and draft an authoritative research argument paper.

modules.title: Desire, Illusion, and Cross-Cultural Identity
modules.description: Students read, discuss, and analyze four literary texts exploring how complex characters struggle to define and shape their own identities against class, gender, and family expectations. Students begin with Tennessee Williams's 'A Streetcar Named Desire' and Jimmy Santiago Baca's poem 'A Daily Joy to Be Alive', analyzing power dynamics, illusion, and emotional rebirth. The module concludes with Nikolai Gogol's 19th-century masterpiece 'The Overcoat' and Jhumpa Lahiri's contemporary novel 'The Namesake', examining immigrant alienation, generational inheritance, and the names we carry.
